title: Incidents, investigation and learning
blurb: Report near misses and incidents, know when MNSI investigates, meet the duty of candour, and share learning with families under PSIRF.
question: A woman is readmitted with a pelvic infection after a swab was left in her vagina following perineal repair. What must the trust and the midwife do under the duty of candour?

teach.body: SPM 5.2 asks midwives to identify, report and critically reflect on near misses, critical incidents, major incidents and serious adverse events. SPM 5.3 adds working with women, families and colleagues to share feedback and learning from both positive and adverse outcomes. In plain English: every incident and near miss is information about how the system works. Reporting it honestly, and involving the family, is how care gets safer.

teach.caption: Learn from Patient Safety Events (LFPSE) replaced the NRLS on 30 June 2024.

teach.body: The Patient Safety Incident Response Framework replaced the 2015 Serious Incident Framework and is a contractual requirement for NHS providers, including maternity. Its four aims are compassionate engagement and involvement of those affected; system-based approaches to learning; considered and proportionate responses; and supportive oversight. In plain English: fewer box-ticking investigations, more real learning about why things happened, with families and staff involved.

teach.h: Who investigates a maternity death or injury
head: Route
Covers
Key feature
rows: Baby deaths from 22 weeks to 28 days
Term labour: stillbirth, death or brain injury in week 1
Maternal death in pregnancy or 42 days after
teach.caption: MNSI does not place blame on individuals or investigate individual staff; the trust implements its recommendations.

teach.body: The professional duty (Code 14) applies to every midwife: be open and candid when things go wrong, put the situation right, explain fully and promptly, and apologise. The statutory duty (regulation 20, England) applies to the provider when a notifiable safety incident occurs: an unintended or unexpected incident that could result, or appears to have resulted, in death, severe harm, moderate harm or prolonged psychological harm.
teach.cite: NMC Code 14; Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regs 2014 reg 20

teach.caption: An apology is 'an expression of sorrow or regret'. It is not of itself an admission of negligence (Compensation Act 2006 s2).

teach.body: Mia is readmitted with a pelvic infection; a swab left after her perineal repair is removed. This is moderate harm: an unplanned readmission. Midwife Esther, who did the swab count, and the senior midwife speak to Mia in person that day, tell her what happened, say sorry, and explain the review. The trust follows up in writing. Esther reports it on the incident system and reflects with her supervisor. Mia is invited to contribute to the learning response.
teach.cite: Reg 20; NMC/GMC Openness and honesty; PSIRF

items.label: e.g. unplanned readmission or return to theatre

teach.text: You do not wait for the investigation to finish before telling the woman what happened. Candour starts as soon as reasonably practicable; the investigation findings follow. And saying sorry is not admitting liability.

items: Report near misses and incidents on the local system (LFPSE nationally); reflect on them (SPM 5.2).
PSIRF replaced the Serious Incident Framework; four aims, including compassionate engagement of those affected.
MNSI: term labour with intrapartum stillbirth, early neonatal death or severe brain injury, and maternal deaths; independent and no blame.
Reg 20: in person as soon as reasonably practicable, true account and apology, then in writing, with records kept.
Moderate harm includes unplanned readmission; prolonged psychological harm lasts at least 28 days.

summary: You can now tell a near miss from an incident, report both, and recognise which events go to MNSI and PMRT. You can also carry out the professional and statutory duty of candour and involve families in learning under PSIRF.

A.q: Which framework replaced the Serious Incident Framework for responding to patient safety incidents in the NHS in England?
options: The duty of candour regulations
The National Reporting and Learning System
The Perinatal Mortality Review Tool
The Patient Safety Incident Response Framework
A.why: PSIRF replaced the Serious Incident Framework (2015) and is contractual for NHS providers, including maternity.

whyNot.0: The duty of candour regulations govern openness with patients, not incident response.
whyNot.1: The NRLS was a reporting system, since replaced by LFPSE.
whyNot.2: PMRT reviews perinatal deaths; it is not the incident response framework.

A.q: A midwife draws up the wrong dose of a medicine for a woman but realises before giving it. What should she do?
options: Report it as a near miss on the local system
Take no action as no harm occurred
Tell the woman she nearly had an error
Inform the NMC of the near miss
A.why: SPM 5.2: identify, report and reflect on near misses. Near misses are reported under local policy; whether to tell the woman is a matter of professional judgement.

whyNot.1: Near misses must be reported so the system can learn.
whyNot.2: Telling the woman is a judgement for near misses; reporting is the required step.
whyNot.3: A near miss is not a matter for the regulator.

A.q: Under the statutory duty of candour, what does an apology mean?
options: An admission that the trust was negligent
An expression of sorrow or regret
A written offer of compensation
A statement of who was at fault
A.why: Regulation 20 defines apology as an expression of sorrow or regret in respect of a notifiable safety incident.

whyNot.0: An apology is not of itself an admission of negligence.
whyNot.2: Compensation is not part of the apology.
whyNot.3: The apology does not assign blame to an individual.

B.q: Which of these events in an English trust should be referred to Maternity and Newborn Safety Investigations?
options: A stillbirth at 30 weeks, before labour began
A third-degree tear after an instrumental birth
Brain injury on day 2 after labour at 39 weeks
Readmission with a wound infection after caesarean
B.why: MNSI investigates babies born after labour at 37 weeks or more with intrapartum stillbirth, early neonatal death or potential severe brain injury diagnosed in the first 7 days, and maternal deaths.

whyNot.0: An antepartum stillbirth at 30 weeks does not meet the MNSI criteria; it is reviewed with PMRT.
whyNot.1: A third-degree tear is managed through the local incident process.
whyNot.3: A wound infection readmission is a local incident, not an MNSI case.

B.q: A woman has had an incident that caused moderate harm. The investigation will take several weeks. When should she first be told what happened?
options: As soon as reasonably practicable
When the investigation report is ready
At her six-week postnatal check
If she makes a formal complaint
B.why: Reg 20 requires notification as soon as reasonably practicable after becoming aware; NMC/GMC guidance says do not wait for the investigation.

whyNot.1: Waiting for the report delays the duty; findings are shared later.
whyNot.2: A routine check is not the trigger for candour.
whyNot.3: Candour does not depend on a complaint.

B.q: A midwife is worried that saying sorry to a woman after an error will be used against her. What is the most accurate advice?
options: Say sorry in writing but not in person
An apology is not of itself admitting negligence
Leave the apology to the trust's legal team
Avoid apologising until the review is complete
B.why: Compensation Act 2006 s2: an apology is not of itself an admission of negligence. NMC/GMC guidance adds that it may show insight.

whyNot.0: Reg 20 requires notification in person, with an apology, before the written follow-up.
whyNot.2: The professional duty to apologise is personal, not delegated to lawyers.
whyNot.3: Delaying the apology breaches the duty to be open promptly.

C.q: After a traumatic emergency birth with an unexpected incident, a woman develops psychological distress. For how long must it last to count as prolonged psychological harm under the duty of candour?
options: At least 7 continuous days
At least 14 continuous days
At least 28 continuous days
At least 42 continuous days
C.why: Prolonged psychological harm and prolonged pain are defined as lasting, or likely to last, at least 28 continuous days.

whyNot.0: 7 days is shorter than the regulation threshold.
whyNot.1: 14 days is shorter than the regulation threshold.
whyNot.3: 42 days is longer than the regulation threshold.

C.q: A trust is designing its response to a series of postpartum haemorrhage incidents. Which approach best reflects the aims of PSIRF?
options: A root cause investigation of each incident
Identifying the staff involved in each case
Adding each incident to the risk register
Proportionate, system-based learning with families
C.why: PSIRF's aims are compassionate engagement of those affected, system-based learning, considered and proportionate responses, and supportive oversight.

whyNot.0: Investigating every incident the same way is the model PSIRF moved away from.
whyNot.1: Focusing on individuals is not system-based learning.
whyNot.2: Logging risks does not deliver learning or engagement.

C.q: A midwife involved in an intrapartum stillbirth at 40 weeks is anxious that the MNSI investigation will decide whether she was at fault. What should she be told?
options: MNSI decides whether to refer her to the NMC
MNSI does not investigate individual staff
MNSI reports her actions to the coroner
MNSI makes recommendations about her employment
C.why: MNSI does not place blame on individuals or investigate individual staff; it makes safety recommendations, which the trust implements.

whyNot.0: MNSI is not a fitness to practise route.
whyNot.2: MNSI's investigation is not a report on an individual to the coroner.
whyNot.3: Employment matters are not part of MNSI's remit.

reteach.title: Report, tell, learn
reteach.question: What three things follow every incident in maternity care?

blocks.body: Report: every near miss and incident goes on the local system. Tell: when harm reaches the woman, be open with her promptly and say sorry; for moderate harm or worse the provider follows regulation 20. Learn: PSIRF looks at the system, MNSI and PMRT add independent and perinatal review, and families are involved throughout.

blocks.text: No harm does not mean no report. Near misses are the cheapest learning there is.

explain.body: Learn from Patient Safety Events (LFPSE) replaced the National Reporting and Learning System, which was decommissioned on 30 June 2024. Staff report through their trust's local system.

test.q: Which national system replaced the National Reporting and Learning System for recording patient safety events in England?
options: The Serious Incident Framework
Learn from Patient Safety Events
The Yellow Card scheme
Maternity Services Data Set
test.why: LFPSE replaced the NRLS, which was decommissioned on 30 June 2024.

whyNot.0: The Serious Incident Framework was replaced by PSIRF, not a reporting system.
whyNot.2: Yellow Card reports adverse drug reactions to the MHRA.
whyNot.3: The Maternity Services Data Set is routine activity data, not incident reporting.

explain.body: Never Events are wholly preventable because strong systemic protective barriers are available nationally and should have been implemented by all providers. They are recorded on LFPSE with learning responses under PSIRF.

test.q: What makes an incident a Never Event?
options: It caused the death of a patient
It was carried out deliberately by staff
National barriers should have prevented it
It has happened more than once in a trust
test.why: Never Events are wholly preventable because guidance or safety recommendations providing strong systemic barriers are available nationally.

whyNot.0: A Never Event need not cause death.
whyNot.1: Deliberate harm is a separate matter; Never Events are about failed barriers.
whyNot.3: One occurrence is enough; frequency is not the definition.

explain.body: After the in-person notification and apology, reg 20 requires a written notification with the same information, the results of any enquiries and an apology, with copies kept.

test.q: After a woman has been told in person about a notifiable safety incident, what does regulation 20 require next?
options: A written notification to her
A report to the NMC
A press statement
A referral to the coroner
test.why: Reg 20: the in-person notification is followed by a written notification, and records are kept.

whyNot.1: The NMC is not notified under reg 20.
whyNot.2: Candour is to the relevant person, not the press.
whyNot.3: Coroner referral relates to certain deaths, not to candour.

explain.body: Ockenden asked for investigation reports to be shared with families in plain language. PMRT produces a plain-language explanation of why a baby died and any implications for future pregnancies.

test.q: Following an investigation into a woman's care, how should the findings be shared with her family?
options: As the technical clinical report
In a summary for her GP to pass on
Through the trust's legal department
In plain language they can understand
test.why: Ockenden asked that reports be shared with families in plain language; PMRT also produces a plain-language explanation for parents.

whyNot.0: A technical report alone is not accessible to families.
whyNot.1: Findings are shared with the family directly, not through the GP.
whyNot.2: Sharing learning is a clinical and governance responsibility, not a legal one.
